title: CORNER C4 Spec: The Hosted Platform
summary: C4 build spec. Docker container per client, provisioning API, WebSocket bridge, OTA updates, admin panel, data isolation, relay bridge, onboarding flow, scaling path, cost model. The thing people pay for.
content:
CORNER C4 Spec: The Hosted Platform

Author: Steve (AI Advisory Lead) Date: 2026-03-16 Depends on: C3 complete (WebSocket, three modes, character movement, mobile PWA) Unlocks: C5 (furniture marketplace, XP UI, social layer, skills marketplace)

What C3 Delivered

C3 proved everything on localhost. WebSocket real-time, three modes, character movement, mobile PWA. Corner feels alive on Patrik's machine. One user, one instance, localhost.

C3 answered: "Does this feel like a game?" Yes.

C4 answers: "Can someone else use this?" Yes. And they pay for it.

What C4 Is

C4 is the hosted product. The thing people pay $3-5k/month for. Everything that turns Patrik's local Corner into a multi-client platform where AOM spins up an isolated AI office for every customer.

C4 North Star: A plumber in Phoenix signs up, goes through onboarding, describes their dream office, and within 5 minutes is chatting with their AI team in a fully provisioned, isolated environment. AOM did nothing manual. The pipeline handled it.

1. Docker Container Architecture

The Principle

One Docker container per client. Complete isolation. Each client gets the same system Patrik runs, not a subset. Their own Claude Code instance, their own context files, their own agents, their own relay.

Container Template

Every client container is built from the same base image. The corner-client image.

# corner-client base image
FROM node:20-slim

# System dependencies
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y \
  git \
  python3 \
  chromium \
  && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*

# Claude Code CLI
RUN npm install -g @anthropic-ai/claude-code

# WebSocket bridge server
COPY ws-bridge/ /opt/corner/ws-bridge/
RUN cd /opt/corner/ws-bridge && npm ci --production

# Relay scripts
COPY relay/ /opt/corner/relay/

# Skill sync agent
COPY skill-sync/ /opt/corner/skill-sync/

# Health check endpoint
COPY healthcheck/ /opt/corner/healthcheck/

# Entry point: starts WS bridge + CC session manager + healthcheck
COPY entrypoint.sh /opt/corner/entrypoint.sh
RUN chmod +x /opt/corner/entrypoint.sh

# Client workspace gets mounted as a volume
VOLUME /workspace

# Ports
EXPOSE 3001  # WebSocket bridge
EXPOSE 3002  # Health check HTTP

ENTRYPOINT ["/opt/corner/entrypoint.sh"]

What's in the Container

Component Purpose Location
Claude Code CLI The AI brain. Real CC with full tool access. Global npm install
WebSocket Bridge Translates CC output to WebSocket events for the dashboard /opt/corner/ws-bridge/
Relay System File-based relay for CC to read/write messages /opt/corner/relay/
Skill Sync Agent Pulls latest skills from AOM's skill repo on update signal /opt/corner/skill-sync/
Health Check HTTP endpoint for fleet monitoring /opt/corner/healthcheck/
Chromium For Playwright/browser automation tasks System package
Git For version control of client context files System package

What's NOT in the Container

  • No frontend. The dashboard is hosted on Vercel. The container is backend only.
  • No Supabase. Supabase is shared infrastructure, not per-container.
  • No direct internet access (except for the Anthropic API and AOM's update server). Network policy enforced.

Client Workspace Volume

Each container gets a persistent volume mounted at /workspace. This is the client's "repo" (equivalent to AOM-EA for Patrik).

/workspace/
  CLAUDE.md                    # Client's system prompt (AOM-templated)
  context/
    me.md                      # From onboarding Step 3
    work.md                    # From onboarding Step 4
    team.md                    # From onboarding Step 5
    goals.md                   # From onboarding Step 6
    current-priorities.md      # Auto-maintained by agents
    current-work.md            # Compaction-safe checkpoint
    relay-inbox.jsonl          # Messages from dashboard chat
    relay-outbox.jsonl         # Responses back to dashboard
  projects/
    [agent-slug]/
      AGENT.md                 # Agent definition
      latest-result.md         # Latest output
      last-conversation.md     # Continuity file
  decisions/
    log.md                     # Decision log
  .claude/
    skills/                    # Skills directory (synced from AOM)
    settings.json              # CC settings

Resource Limits

Per container, enforced by Docker:

Resource Limit Rationale
CPU 2 cores CC is CPU-light (API calls, not compute). 2 cores handles concurrent agents.
Memory 4 GB CC process + Node.js WS bridge + Playwright. 4 GB is generous for the workload.
Disk (workspace volume) 10 GB Context files, agent outputs, git history. 10 GB lasts years for a typical client.
Disk (temp) 5 GB Playwright screenshots, temporary build artifacts. Cleaned daily.
Network Anthropic API + AOM update server only No arbitrary outbound. Allowlisted domains via iptables rules.
Open files 65536 Node.js + chokidar watchers need headroom.

Why these limits work: CC's workload is overwhelmingly I/O-bound (API calls to Anthropic). It doesn't need GPU or heavy CPU. The bottleneck is Anthropic's response time, not container compute. At 2 cores / 4 GB, a single Hetzner CX52 (16 vCPU, 32 GB RAM) fits ~8 containers comfortably, or ~16 containers with some oversubscription (most containers are idle at any given moment).

Networking

Internet
   |
   v
+------------------+
| Caddy / Traefik  |  <-- Reverse proxy, TLS termination, WebSocket routing
| (port 443)       |
+------------------+
   |
   +---> container-client-001:3001  (WebSocket)
   +---> container-client-002:3001  (WebSocket)
   +---> container-client-003:3001  (WebSocket)
   ...
  • Reverse proxy: Caddy (preferred for auto-TLS) or Traefik.
  • Routing: Each client gets a subdomain: {org-slug}.ws.corner.app. Reverse proxy routes to the correct container based on subdomain.
  • TLS: Auto-provisioned via Let's Encrypt. Caddy handles this natively.
  • Internal network: Docker bridge network. Containers cannot communicate with each other. Only the reverse proxy can reach container ports.
  • DNS: Wildcard A record *.ws.corner.app pointing to the server IP. New clients work immediately without DNS changes.

2. Provisioning API

What Triggers Provisioning

The onboarding wizard (Step 8, "Meet Your Team") triggers provisioning. By the time the client finishes describing their dream office, the backend is already spinning up their container.

Provisioning Flow

Client completes onboarding Step 6 (Goals)
          |
          v
Frontend calls POST /api/onboarding/provision
          |
          v
Provisioning API (AOM server):
  1. Create organization record in Supabase
  2. Create workspace volume with context files
     (me.md, work.md, team.md, goals.md from onboarding answers)
  3. Generate CLAUDE.md from template + client data
  4. Configure agent roster based on business stage
  5. Pull latest corner-client Docker image
  6. Create + start container with workspace volume mounted
  7. Wait for health check (container reports ready)
  8. Register WebSocket endpoint in Supabase vm_endpoints table
  9. Return { status: "ready", ws_endpoint: "org-slug.ws.corner.app" }
          |
          v
Meanwhile: Gemini generates room sprites (parallel, async)
          |
          v
Frontend: Room reveal animation plays as rooms generate
          |
          v
Client is live. Chat works. Agents are ready.

Provisioning API Endpoints

All endpoints authenticated via AOM admin JWT (not client-accessible).

POST /api/provision/create Create a new client environment.

// Request
{
  "organization_id": "uuid",
  "org_slug": "phoenix-cpa-group",
  "plan": "platform",
  "context_files": {
    "me": "# About John\n...",
    "work": "# Phoenix CPA Group\n...",
    "team": "# Team\n...",
    "goals": "# Goals\n..."
  },
  "agent_roster": ["email_triage", "lead_response", "calendar", "operations"],
  "anthropic_api_key": "sk-ant-..."
}

// Response
{
  "status": "provisioning",
  "container_id": "corner-phoenix-cpa-group",
  "ws_endpoint": "phoenix-cpa-group.ws.corner.app",
  "estimated_ready_seconds": 120
}

GET /api/provision/status/{org_slug} Check provisioning progress.

{
  "status": "ready",  // "provisioning" | "ready" | "failed" | "stopped"
  "container_id": "corner-phoenix-cpa-group",
  "ws_endpoint": "phoenix-cpa-group.ws.corner.app",
  "uptime_seconds": 3600,
  "health": "healthy"
}

POST /api/provision/restart/{org_slug} Restart a client container. Preserves workspace volume.

POST /api/provision/destroy/{org_slug} Stop and remove a client container. Workspace volume archived (not deleted) for 90 days.

Provisioning Timing

Step Duration Notes
Create Supabase records ~1s API calls
Write context files to volume ~2s Disk I/O
Generate CLAUDE.md ~1s Template rendering
Configure agent roster ~2s Write AGENT.md files
Pull Docker image (cached) ~0s Image is pre-pulled on server
Start container ~5-10s Docker start + Node.js boot + CC initialization
Health check passes ~15-30s CC session initializes, reads context files
Register WS endpoint ~1s Supabase write
Total ~30-45s Well under the 5-minute target

The client spends ~60-90s on Step 7 (describing their dream office) and ~30-60s watching room generation. By the time they see "Meet Your Team" at Step 8, the container is ready.

Agent Roster Configuration

Based on business stage from onboarding Step 2:

"I have a business" (established):

  • Operations agent (Mom equivalent)
  • Calendar/scheduling agent
  • Email triage agent
  • Lead response agent
  • 1-2 industry-specific agents based on business type

"I'm building one" (startup):

  • Strategy agent (Steve equivalent)
  • Market research agent (Alex equivalent)
  • Builder agent (Bobby equivalent)
  • Operations agent

"Just an idea" (zero stage):

  • Strategy agent (validates the concept)
  • Market research agent
  • Operations agent (lightweight, guides next steps)

Each agent type has a template AGENT.md in AOM's skill repo. The provisioning API copies and customizes these templates with client-specific context.

3. WebSocket Bridge (VM to Browser)

Architecture

The WebSocket bridge runs inside each container. It connects the CC process to the client's browser via WebSocket.

Browser (Vercel frontend)
        |
        | wss://org-slug.ws.corner.app
        v
Caddy reverse proxy (server)
        |
        | ws://container:3001
        v
+----------------------------------+
| Container: WS Bridge Server      |
|                                   |
|  File Watcher (chokidar)         |
|    watches: relay-outbox.jsonl   |
|    watches: agent status files   |
|    watches: latest-result.md     |
|                                   |
|  CC Session Manager              |
|    spawns: claude-code sessions  |
|    routes: chat messages to CC   |
|    captures: CC output events    |
|                                   |
|  WebSocket Server (ws library)   |
|    authenticates: Supabase JWT   |
|    broadcasts: events to client  |
|    receives: chat messages       |
+----------------------------------+

Authentication Flow

  1. Client logs into Corner dashboard (Vercel frontend) via Supabase Auth
  2. Frontend receives Supabase JWT
  3. Frontend opens WebSocket to wss://org-slug.ws.corner.app
  4. JWT sent in the WebSocket handshake (via Sec-WebSocket-Protocol header or initial auth message)
  5. WS Bridge Server validates JWT by calling Supabase's JWT verification endpoint
  6. If valid: connection accepted, client receives events
  7. If invalid/expired: connection rejected with 4001 close code
// WS Bridge: auth verification
async function verifyClient(jwt) {
  // Decode JWT, verify signature against Supabase JWT secret
  const decoded = jwt.verify(token, process.env.SUPABASE_JWT_SECRET);

  // Verify org_id matches this container's org
  const userOrgId = decoded.app_metadata?.organization_id;
  if (userOrgId !== process.env.ORG_ID) {
    return { valid: false, reason: "wrong_org" };
  }

  // Check role has access
  const role = decoded.app_metadata?.role;
  if (!["admin", "member", "viewer", "super_admin"].includes(role)) {
    return { valid: false, reason: "insufficient_role" };
  }

  return { valid: true, orgId: userOrgId, role, userId: decoded.sub };
}

Event Protocol

Same protocol from C3, now over the internet instead of localhost:

Client to Server (browser to container):

{
  "type": "chat_message",
  "agent": "bobby",
  "content": "What's the status on the website?",
  "message_id": "uuid-v4",
  "timestamp": "2026-03-16T14:30:00Z"
}

{
  "type": "task_create",
  "agent": "bobby",
  "text": "Fix the contact form",
  "position": 0,
  "timestamp": "2026-03-16T14:31:00Z"
}

{
  "type": "task_reorder",
  "agent": "bobby",
  "task_id": "uuid",
  "new_position": 2,
  "timestamp": "2026-03-16T14:32:00Z"
}

Server to Client (container to browser): Same events as C3 spec: agent_state_change, token_stream, task_complete, task_created, handoff, error_recovery, system_status. Plus:

{
  "type": "connection_info",
  "container_id": "corner-phoenix-cpa-group",
  "uptime_seconds": 3600,
  "agents_online": 4,
  "cc_version": "1.2.3",
  "skills_version": "2026-03-16-001",
  "timestamp": "2026-03-16T14:30:00Z"
}

{
  "type": "sync_state",
  "agents": [
    { "slug": "email-triage", "status": "idle", "current_task": null },
    { "slug": "lead-response", "status": "working", "current_task": "Responding to John Smith inquiry" },
    { "slug": "calendar", "status": "idle", "current_task": null },
    { "slug": "operations", "status": "thinking", "current_task": "Analyzing weekly schedule" }
  ],
  "timestamp": "2026-03-16T14:30:00Z"
}

The sync_state event fires on initial connection and every 30 seconds as a heartbeat. Ensures the dashboard stays accurate even if individual events are missed.

Connection Management

Scenario Behavior
Clean connection JWT validated, connection_info + sync_state sent immediately
JWT expired WS Bridge sends 4001 close. Frontend refreshes JWT via Supabase, reconnects.
Network drop Client auto-reconnects (exponential backoff: 1s, 2s, 4s, 8s, max 30s). On reconnect, sync_state replays current state.
Container restart All connections close. Frontend auto-reconnects. Shows "Reconnecting..." toast (not error).
Multiple tabs Each tab gets its own WS connection. Events broadcast to all. No conflicts.
Viewer role Can receive all events. Chat messages and task mutations rejected with {"type": "error", "code": "insufficient_permissions"}.
Super admin Can connect to any container by passing org_id in the auth payload. Used for AOM admin panel.

Latency Targets (Hosted)

C3 targets on localhost were: <500ms ack, <2s first token, <1s status updates.

For hosted (over the internet), add network overhead:

Metric C3 (localhost) C4 (hosted) Budget
Acknowledgment <500ms <800ms +300ms network round-trip
First token <2s <3s +1s for network + CC cold start
Status updates <1s <1.5s +500ms network
Heartbeat 30s 30s Same
Reconnect Instant <5s Network detection + backoff

These are conservative. A Hetzner server in Ashburn, VA (US East) to Phoenix is ~40ms round-trip. The bottleneck will always be Anthropic's API response time, not AOM's infrastructure.

4. Over-the-Air Skill Updates

The Principle

AOM pushes improvements to all clients at once. New skills, agent personality updates, system patches, performance optimizations. Clients don't manage updates. They just see their agents getting better.

Update Architecture

AOM Skill Repo (GitHub: mrg33k/corner-skills)
          |
          v
AOM pushes git tag / webhook triggers
          |
          v
Update Server (runs on the AOM fleet server)
          |
          +---> Signal container-001: "pull skills v2026-03-16-002"
          +---> Signal container-002: "pull skills v2026-03-16-002"
          +---> Signal container-003: "pull skills v2026-03-16-002"
          ...
          |
          v
Each container's Skill Sync Agent:
  1. git pull from corner-skills repo
  2. Copy updated skills to /workspace/.claude/skills/
  3. Copy updated AGENT.md templates (if agent personality updates)
  4. Write update receipt to /workspace/context/system-updates.log
  5. Report success to Update Server
  6. Broadcast WS event: { "type": "system_status", "message": "Skills updated" }

What Gets Updated (and What Doesn't)

Asset Updatable OTA? How
Skills (.claude/skills/) Yes Git pull from corner-skills repo
CLAUDE.md template sections Yes Merge AOM template blocks with client customizations
AGENT.md personality traits Yes (opt-in) Client can lock agent personalities. Default: accept updates.
Relay scripts Yes Versioned, replaced atomically
WS Bridge server Yes (requires restart) New image pulled, container restarted with rolling update
Client context files (me.md, work.md) NEVER These are the client's data. Never touched by updates.
Client decisions/log.md NEVER Client's decision history. Immutable.
Client agent latest-result.md NEVER Agent work output. Client owns this.

Update Types

Hot update (no restart): Skills, AGENT.md personality, relay scripts. Applied while container is running. CC picks up new skills on next invocation.

Warm update (graceful restart): WS Bridge server, healthcheck, entry point changes. Container waits for active CC sessions to complete (timeout: 60s), then restarts. Client sees "Updating your office..." for ~30 seconds.

Cold update (new image): Base image changes (Node.js version, system deps, CC CLI version). Requires pulling new image and recreating container. Workspace volume preserved. Client offline for ~60-90 seconds. Scheduled during low-activity windows (2-4 AM client's timezone).

Update Rollback

Every update is tagged with a version. If update causes issues:

  1. AOM admin panel shows health check failures for affected containers
  2. Admin clicks "rollback" on the update
  3. Containers revert to previous skill/config version via git revert
  4. Update Server signals all containers to pull the rollback

Rollback is automated for cold updates: if a container fails health check after image update, it automatically reverts to the previous image.

Versioning

Skills repo uses dated version tags: v2026-03-16-001, v2026-03-16-002.

Each container tracks its current version in /workspace/context/system-version.json:

{
  "skills_version": "v2026-03-16-002",
  "ws_bridge_version": "1.4.0",
  "base_image": "corner-client:2026-03-16",
  "last_update": "2026-03-16T08:00:00Z",
  "update_history": [
    { "version": "v2026-03-16-001", "applied_at": "2026-03-16T04:00:00Z", "type": "hot" },
    { "version": "v2026-03-16-002", "applied_at": "2026-03-16T08:00:00Z", "type": "hot" }
  ]
}

5. AOM Admin Panel

What It Is

A web interface for AOM (Patrik, Ash, and the team) to manage the entire client fleet. See every container, monitor health, push updates, troubleshoot issues. This is the "command center for the command centers."

The admin panel is NOT part of the Corner product. It's AOM's internal tool. Clients never see it.

Access

  • Separate auth context from client dashboard
  • Restricted to super_admin role in Supabase
  • Accessible at admin.corner.app (or /admin on the AOM site during MVP)
  • 2FA mandatory for all admin access

Steffen Design Need: Admin Panel

The admin panel needs to feel like a control room. Not a boring CRUD dashboard.

6. Client Data Isolation

Layers of Isolation

Client data is isolated at four layers. Defense in depth.

Layer 1: Container isolation (Docker)

  • Each client runs in a separate Docker container
  • No shared filesystem between containers
  • No shared process space
  • Docker bridge network prevents container-to-container communication
  • Even if one container is compromised, it cannot access another client's data

Layer 2: Volume isolation (filesystem)

  • Each client's workspace is a separate Docker volume
  • Volumes are not accessible from other containers
  • Volume data encrypted at rest (LUKS or filesystem-level encryption on the host)
  • Backup volumes are encrypted with per-client keys

Layer 3: Network isolation (firewall)

  • Containers can only reach:
    • Anthropic API (api.anthropic.com)
    • AOM's update server (internal)
    • AOM's Supabase instance (for event sync)
  • All other outbound traffic blocked by iptables rules
  • Inbound: only the reverse proxy can reach container port 3001

Layer 4: Database isolation (Supabase RLS)

  • Client visualization data in Supabase is protected by Row-Level Security
  • Every query is scoped to the authenticated user's organization_id
  • Super admins can query across orgs for fleet management
  • Audit log records all cross-tenant queries

Secret Management

Secret Storage Access
Client's Anthropic API key Container env var (Docker secrets for production) Only the container's CC process
Supabase JWT secret Server env var (shared, one Supabase project) WS Bridge for JWT validation
Client's context files Container workspace volume Only the container's processes
AOM admin credentials Separate auth, hardware key (YubiKey) Patrik, Ash only

Data Lifecycle

Event What Happens to Data
Client signs up Workspace volume created, context files written
Client uses the product Context files grow, agent outputs accumulate, events sync to Supabase
Client downgrades/pauses Container stopped. Volume preserved. Supabase data preserved.
Client cancels Container stopped. Volume archived to encrypted cold storage. Supabase data soft-deleted. 90-day retention.
90 days after cancellation Volume permanently deleted. Supabase records purged. Audit log entries preserved (compliance).
Client requests data export Full workspace volume zipped and sent. Supabase records exported as JSON.

Compliance Mapping

Requirement (from Elon's security architecture) How C4 Addresses It
FTC Safeguards Rule: MFA Supabase Auth with 2FA mandatory for all access
FTC: Encryption in transit TLS on all WebSocket connections (wss://)
FTC: Encryption at rest Volume encryption (LUKS). Supabase uses encrypted storage.
FTC: Access controls Container isolation + RLS + role-based permissions
IRS Pub 4557: Vendor security Container isolation + audit logging + encrypted storage
SOC 2 Security: Access logging audit_log table (append-only, immutable) + container access logs
SOC 2 Availability: Uptime Health checks + auto-restart + admin alerts
SOC 2 Confidentiality: Data isolation 4-layer isolation model above

7. Relay Bridge (Dashboard Chat Protocol)

Why Not Telegram

Clients don't use Telegram. Their game dashboard chat IS the relay. The dashboard chat bar sends messages to the container via WebSocket, and the container's relay system feeds them to CC.

The Protocol: Browser to CC

1. Client types message in chat bar
2. Frontend sends WS message:
   { "type": "chat_message", "agent": "operations", "content": "What happened today?", "message_id": "uuid" }

3. WS Bridge receives message
4. WS Bridge writes to relay-inbox.jsonl:
   { "id": "uuid", "content": "What happened today?", "agent": "operations", "timestamp": "...", "status": "pending" }

5. CC's hook system (same as Patrik's relay-hook.sh) detects pending message
6. CC processes the message with the specified agent

7. CC writes response to relay-outbox.jsonl:
   { "id": "uuid", "response": "Today your team handled 12 emails...", "agent": "operations", "timestamp": "..." }

8. WS Bridge's file watcher detects new outbox line
9. WS Bridge broadcasts via WebSocket:
   { "type": "token_stream", "agent": "operations", "token": "Today", "message_id": "uuid", "timestamp": "..." }
   { "type": "token_stream", "agent": "operations", "token": " your", ... }
   { "type": "token_stream", "agent": "operations", "token": " team", ... }
   ...
   { "type": "chat_complete", "agent": "operations", "message_id": "uuid", "full_response": "Today your team handled 12 emails...", "timestamp": "..." }

10. Frontend renders tokens word-by-word in chat bubble + speech bubble above agent sprite

Multi-Agent Chat

Clients can chat with different agents by selecting them in the chat bar or clicking their room.

Each agent has its own conversation thread. The WS Bridge routes messages to the correct CC session based on the agent field.

CC Session Management in the Container:

For C4 MVP, the container runs a single CC session with agent context switching (same as Patrik's main session that can invoke different agents).

For C4.1+, the container runs multiple concurrent CC sessions (one per actively chatting agent), with a session pool:

  • Max 3 concurrent CC sessions per container
  • Sessions idle for >5 minutes are terminated
  • New session spun up when client chats with a new agent
  • Session pool managed by the WS Bridge's CC Session Manager

Chat History

  • All messages (client + agent responses) written to Supabase conversations table
  • Also stored locally in the container's relay files (source of truth for CC context)
  • Supabase copy is for the dashboard to display conversation history on page load
  • When client opens chat with an agent, frontend loads last 50 messages from Supabase, then switches to WebSocket for real-time

Offline Message Handling

If the client sends a message while the container is restarting or offline:

  1. Frontend detects WebSocket disconnection
  2. Message queued in localStorage
  3. Frontend shows: "Your message will be delivered when [Agent] returns."
  4. On reconnect: queued messages sent in order
  5. Agent processes them and responds

8. Onboarding Flow (End to End)

The Full Journey

Client signs up on corner.app (or is referred by AOM after an audit).

Phase 1: Account Creation (30 seconds)

  1. Client clicks "Get Started" on corner.app
  2. Email + password + company name

Phase 2: Business Context (3-5 minutes)

From the product spec, Steps 2-6. One question per screen. Conversational, not a form.

  1. "Do you have a business, or are you building one?" (determines path)
  2. About You (builds me.md): name, role, one-sentence about the business
  3. Your Business (builds work.md): what you do, services, clients, team size, tools, biggest time drain
  4. Your Team (builds team.md): who else should have access, who handles what

Each answer is saved to Supabase immediately. If client drops off, they resume where they left off.

  1. "Describe your dream office."
  2. Client types: "Modern tech startup with lots of plants"
  3. System sends description to Gemini 2.5 Flash Image model

  6. Generated room PNGs saved to Supabase Storage

Meanwhile: Provisioning API is triggered at step 11. Container starts spinning up while rooms generate. By the time rooms are done, the container is ready.

Phase 4: Meet Your Team (30 seconds)

  1. The isometric world appears for the first time
  2. Rooms populate one by one with snap-into-place animation
  3. Each agent introduces themselves: speech bubble greeting above their room
    • Operations: "Morning, [Name]. I'll keep everything running smooth."
    • Email Triage: "I've got your inbox. You focus on the big stuff."
    • Calendar: "Your schedule's in good hands. Just tell me when."
    • Lead Response: "Someone reaches out? I'm on it before they look away."
  4. "Welcome to your Corner" banner
  5. Chat bar pulses gently, inviting first interaction
  6. Client clicks any room or types in chat bar

Phase 5: First Value (<2 minutes)

  1. Agent responds to first message with something immediately useful:
    • If they mentioned a pain point in onboarding: "You mentioned [X] is your biggest time drain. Here's what I'd do about it..."
    • If they have a team: "I see you have [N] team members. Let me set up task tracking for [Name]..."
    • Generic: "I've read through your goals. Here's my recommended first three priorities..."
  2. This is the "aha" moment. The agent knows the client's context from onboarding.

Clients who already went through AOM's AI Operations Audit ($2,500):

9. Scaling

Phase 1: Single Server (Clients 1-50)

Hardware: Hetzner dedicated server.

Spec Value Monthly Cost
CPU AMD EPYC, 16 vCPU Included
RAM 64 GB Included
Storage 2x 1TB NVMe (RAID-1) Included
Bandwidth 20 TB Included
Location Ashburn, VA (US East) ~$80-120/month

Capacity math:

Each container: 2 CPU cores, 4 GB RAM. With oversubscription (most containers idle): 3-4x oversubscription on CPU, 1.5x on RAM.

  • CPU: 16 cores / 2 per container = 8 containers at full allocation. With 4x oversubscription: ~32 containers.
  • RAM: 64 GB / 4 per container = 16 containers at full allocation. With 1.5x oversubscription: ~24 containers.
  • RAM is the bottleneck. Upgrade to 128 GB for ~$40/mo more: ~48 containers.

Container orchestration: Docker Compose for Phase 1. Simple, Patrik and Ash can manage it.

docker-compose.yml structure:

version: "3.8"

services:
  caddy:
    image: caddy:2-alpine
    ports:
      - "443:443"
      - "80:80"
    volumes:
      - ./Caddyfile:/etc/caddy/Caddyfile
      - caddy_data:/data
    restart: unless-stopped

  provisioner:
    image: corner-provisioner:latest
    volumes:
      - /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock
      - /data/workspaces:/data/workspaces
    environment:
      - SUPABASE_URL=${SUPABASE_URL}
      - SUPABASE_SERVICE_KEY=${SUPABASE_SERVICE_KEY}
    restart: unless-stopped

  updater:
    image: corner-updater:latest
    volumes:
      - /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock
    environment:
      - SKILLS_REPO_URL=https://github.com/mrg33k/corner-skills.git
      - SKILLS_REPO_TOKEN=${GITHUB_TOKEN}
    restart: unless-stopped

  # Client containers are created dynamically by the provisioner
  # They are NOT defined in docker-compose.yml
  # The provisioner uses the Docker API to create/manage them

volumes:
  caddy_data:

Phase 2: Bigger Server (Clients 50-150)

When the single server fills up:

  1. Upgrade to Hetzner AX162 or similar (32 vCPU, 128 GB RAM): ~$150-200/month
  2. Same Docker Compose setup, just more headroom
  3. If one server isn't enough, add a second server and split clients between them manually

When to move past Phase 2: When manual client-to-server assignment becomes a burden, or when AOM needs auto-scaling for load spikes.

Phase 3: Kubernetes (Clients 150+)

When Docker Compose isn't enough:

Trigger points:

  • More than 2 servers to manage manually
  • Need auto-scaling (container count fluctuates with time of day)
  • Need zero-downtime rolling updates across 150+ containers
  • Need automatic failover (container dies, Kubernetes restarts it on another node)
  • Need resource bin-packing (Kubernetes packs containers efficiently across nodes)

Kubernetes setup:

  • Managed Kubernetes (Hetzner Cloud, DigitalOcean, or AWS EKS)
  • Each client container becomes a Kubernetes Pod
  • StatefulSet for containers (persistent volumes need stable names)
  • Ingress controller (Traefik or nginx-ingress) replaces Caddy for routing
  • Horizontal Pod Autoscaler based on WebSocket connection count
  • Persistent Volumes backed by Hetzner Block Storage or AWS EBS

What changes:

  • Docker Compose replaced by Helm charts
  • Provisioning API talks to Kubernetes API instead of Docker API
  • Health checks become Kubernetes liveness/readiness probes
  • Container restarts are automatic (Kubernetes restart policy)
  • Rolling updates managed by Kubernetes (zero downtime)

What doesn't change:

  • Container image is the same
  • WebSocket protocol is the same
  • Client workspace volumes are the same
  • Skill update mechanism is the same (just signals Pods instead of containers)

Estimated Kubernetes infrastructure cost for 150 clients:

  • 3-4 nodes: ~$400-600/month (Hetzner Cloud)
  • Managed Kubernetes control plane: ~$50/month
  • Block storage for volumes: ~$100/month
  • Total: ~$650-750/month

At $3-5k per client, 150 clients = $450k-750k MRR. Infrastructure at $750/month is <0.2% of revenue.

Scaling Decision Tree

Clients: 1-50
  -> Single Hetzner dedicated server ($80-120/mo)
  -> Docker Compose
  -> Manual management (Patrik/Ash)

Clients: 50-150
  -> Hetzner AX162 ($150-200/mo) or 2 servers
  -> Docker Compose
  -> Still manageable manually

Clients: 150+
  -> Managed Kubernetes ($650-750/mo)
  -> Auto-scaling, auto-failover, rolling updates
  -> Hire a DevOps person or contract it out

Clients: 500+
  -> Multi-region Kubernetes
  -> US East + US West + EU
  -> Full SRE team
  -> But this is a $1.5M+ MRR problem. Nice problem to have.

C4 Build Order

Sequenced for fastest path to first paying client.

Step 1: Container Template (4-5 days)

Build the corner-client Docker image. Get a single container running with CC, WS Bridge, and relay.

  • Dockerfile finalized
  • WS Bridge server (Node.js, ws library, port 3001)
  • Relay scripts (inbox/outbox JSONL, same pattern as AOM-EA)
  • Health check HTTP endpoint (port 3002)
  • Entry point script (starts all services)
  • Test: run container locally, connect to WS from browser, chat with CC
  • Ship: One container works. CC responds via WebSocket.

Step 2: Provisioning API (3-4 days)

Automated container creation. No manual Docker commands.

  • POST /api/provision/create endpoint
  • Writes context files to volume from request payload
  • Generates CLAUDE.md from template
  • Creates and starts container via Docker API
  • Registers WS endpoint in Supabase vm_endpoints
  • Health check polling (wait until ready)
  • GET /api/provision/status endpoint
  • Ship: API call creates a fully provisioned client container.

Step 3: Reverse Proxy + TLS (1-2 days)

WebSocket routing from the internet to containers.

  • Caddy configuration with wildcard TLS
  • Subdomain routing: {org-slug}.ws.corner.app to correct container
  • Dynamic Caddyfile generation (new client = new route)
  • Test: connect to WS from the internet via HTTPS
  • Ship: Client browser can reach their container securely.

Step 4: WebSocket Auth (2-3 days)

Secure the WS connection.

  • JWT validation in WS Bridge
  • Organization ID matching (container only accepts its own org's users)
  • Role-based message filtering (viewers can't send chat messages)
  • Connection rejection with proper close codes
  • Super admin cross-tenant access
  • Ship: Only authenticated, authorized users can connect.

Step 5: Onboarding Wizard (4-5 days)

Client goes from "sign up" to "chatting with agents."

  • Account creation flow (Supabase Auth)
  • One-question-per-screen UI
  • Context file generation from answers
  • Gemini room generation integration
  • Provisioning triggered at "Describe your dream office" step
  • Room reveal animation
  • Agent greeting messages
  • Ship: New user signs up, goes through onboarding, lands in their office.

Step 6: Admin Panel MVP (3-4 days)

AOM can see and manage the fleet.

  • Fleet overview (all containers, status, plan)
  • Client detail view (agents, resources, events, logs)
  • Restart / stop / destroy actions
  • Container log streaming
  • Basic health monitoring
  • Ship: Patrik and Ash can see every client and troubleshoot.

Step 7: OTA Update System (2-3 days)

Push improvements to all clients.

  • Skills repo structure (corner-skills)
  • Skill Sync Agent in container
  • Update Server (signals containers to pull)
  • Version tracking per container
  • Rollback capability
  • Ship: AOM pushes a skill update, all containers get it within 5 minutes.

Step 8: Data Isolation Hardening (2-3 days)

Lock down security.

  • Network policy (iptables rules per container)
  • Volume encryption (LUKS on host)
  • Docker secrets for API keys
  • Audit logging for all admin actions
  • Penetration test the WebSocket endpoint
  • Ship: Security posture ready for CPA clients.

Step 9: Client Management (2-3 days)

Business operations tooling.

  • Client pause/resume (stop container, preserve data)
  • Client offboarding (archive volume, purge Supabase)
  • Data export (zip workspace + JSON export)
  • Usage metrics per client (messages, tasks, response times)
  • Ship: AOM can manage client lifecycle end to end.

Step 10: Dashboard Integration (3-4 days)

Connect the existing C3 dashboard to hosted containers.

  • Frontend WS endpoint resolution: look up org's WS endpoint from Supabase vm_endpoints
  • Replace localhost WS URL with dynamic endpoint
  • Multi-org support in frontend (each user sees their org's data)
  • Login flow: Supabase Auth -> resolve org -> connect to VM -> load game
  • All three modes work against hosted containers
  • Ship: C3 dashboard works against hosted VMs. Full product end to end.

Total estimated build time: 26-36 days (5-7 weeks)
